prompt: Before assigning loads, the trainer watches a squat, a hinge, and a single-leg balance, noting where position breaks down. What should that posture and movement screen be used to do?

options.text: Name the injured tissue and plan treatment for whatever pain the client described in the interview
Identify movement limitations and compensation patterns so programming can be guided
Predict injury so precisely that any activity can be cleared without sending the client to a physician
Read maximal strength and power off the screen score and set working loads from that number

explanation: The squat, hinge, and balance check show where this client loses position so the program can work around those limits. The screen guides exercise choice. It does not diagnose an injury or clear the client for anything.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns a movement screen into a diagnosis and a treatment plan, which is outside what a trainer may decide.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the screen as a precise injury forecast that can replace a physician, which it cannot do.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a posture and movement screen with a strength or power test used to set maximal loads.

prompt: During a strength session, a physician-cleared client with osteoporosis brings a note that bars loaded spinal flexion, then asks to outlaw twisting slams and every squat because a training partner said any core drill or any load will break bone. What should you program?

options.text: Drop weight-bearing walking and impact, on the idea that they speed the loss of bone mineral
Drop progressive resistance, on the idea that any external load is too much for this bone
Keep well-aligned loaded movement and omit only the spinal flexion the physician restricted
Drop balance practice, on the idea that stability drills cause falls and new fractures

explanation: The note bars loaded spinal flexion, so that pattern stays out. Twisting slams and squats were not on the note, and you do not grow the restriction into a longer banned list. Keep the well-aligned loaded movement this cleared client was allowed to do.

distractorExplanations.a: Drops weight-bearing walking, which supports bone, and treats impact as a cause of mineral loss the note never named.
distractorExplanations.b: Invents a ban on every external load. The physician restricted spinal flexion, not the aligned resistance this client was cleared to do.
distractorExplanations.d: Drops balance practice that reduces falls, and treats it as a cause of fractures the note did not list.

prompt: A client with asthma arrives for intervals on a cold dry morning and carries a written action plan plus a reliever inhaler. What should the trainer build into the session?

options.text: A short warm-up and immediate high intensity so the airways adapt faster to hard effort
Extra time in the coldest air so the airways become desensitized before the main intervals
Inhaler use saved for after exercise, and then if symptoms are still present later at home
An extended warm-up, trigger awareness, and inhaler access that follows the written action plan

explanation: This cold-morning interval session needs a longer warm-up, attention to triggers such as cold dry air, and the reliever inhaler available as the written action plan describes. The trainer follows that plan and does not rewrite it.

distractorExplanations.a: Shortens the warm-up and jumps to hard effort, which is the abrupt start that often provokes airway symptoms.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds cold dry air on purpose to desensitize the airways, treating a common trigger as a training tool.
distractorExplanations.c: Hides the inhaler until after the session and possibly until the client is home, instead of keeping it available per the plan.

prompt: Formal physical therapy has just ended after a joint repair, precautions remain on the note, and the client wants last year's full program at the next session. How should this return to training be handled?

options.text: Obtain clearance, respect the listed precautions, and progress while communicating with the care team
Resume the pre-injury program at full intensity the day formal therapy sessions end
Repeat the same therapy drills indefinitely without adding load, range, or task difficulty
Replace any remaining clinical visits with a rehab protocol designed by the trainer alone

explanation: Discharge from therapy is not a green light for last year's loads. Get clearance, keep the precautions still on the note, and progress only while staying in contact with the care team that set those limits.

distractorExplanations.b: Restarts the old program at full intensity the day therapy ends, ignoring precautions that are still listed.
distractorExplanations.c: Freezes the home drills forever and never progresses load or complexity after clearance allows a graded return.
distractorExplanations.d: Replaces clinical care with a trainer-written rehab plan, which steps outside the trainer's scope.

prompt: At a field assessment the trainer measures several skinfold sites with calipers and enters the sum into a published prediction equation. What is that method actually estimating?

options.text: Fat stored around the organs, read directly as a visceral metabolic-risk score
Subcutaneous fat, then an estimated body-fat percentage through a prediction equation
Total body water and lean mass inferred from an electrical current through the tissues
Body fat with accuracy equal to a laboratory DEXA scan and with no technician error

explanation: Calipers pinch subcutaneous fat at the sites, and the sum goes into an equation that estimates body-fat percentage. That is a field estimate with technician error, not a direct read of organ fat or a DEXA result.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a skinfold pinch with a direct measure of visceral fat around the organs.
distractorExplanations.c: Describes bioelectrical impedance, which uses current and body water, not calipers and an equation.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats the field estimate as equal to DEXA and ignores the technician error that comes with skinfolds.

prompt: A cleared client with type 2 diabetes uses medication only a physician adjusts and sometimes feels shaky late in longer workouts. What should teaching cover on those exercise days?

options.text: Choose and administer insulin doses before the session as the trainer sees fit
Skip medical appointments because the training log now replaces clinical follow-up
Monitor for signs of low or high blood sugar around exercise and coordinate with the care plan
Stop every prescribed medicine on the client's own, because workouts will cover the condition

explanation: On these longer days, teach the client to notice signs of low or high blood sugar and to stay aligned with the physician's care plan. Shakiness is a reason to respond within that plan. The trainer does not adjust insulin or other medication.

distractorExplanations.a: Has the trainer choose and give insulin, which is medication advice outside the session and outside scope.
distractorExplanations.b: Cancels medical follow-up and treats the gym log as a substitute for the physician's care.
distractorExplanations.d: Stops prescribed medicine because of exercise, a unilateral change the trainer must not support.

prompt: An older adult with two recent falls can stand on both feet beside a counter but wobbles as soon as the stance gets narrow. How should balance practice progress while support stays available?

options.text: Unstable surfaces first, then the stable floor, then single-leg holds if nothing failed
Eyes-closed stances first, then eyes open, then a wider base once confidence returns
Single-leg stance first, then tandem, then a wide two-foot stance as the last step
Stable two-foot support, then narrower bases, then perturbations when those are safe

explanation: This client already manages a wide stance by the counter and wobbles when the base narrows, so practice starts on that stable two-foot support. Narrow the base next, and add small perturbations only when the earlier steps are safe and a spot is still there.

distractorExplanations.a: Opens on unstable surfaces, the harder setting, instead of a stable floor with support nearby.
distractorExplanations.b: Removes vision first and widens the base later, reversing a progression that should start eyes-open and wide.
distractorExplanations.c: Starts at single-leg and finishes at a wide stance, running the base-of-support steps backward.

prompt: On day one a new member fills out a readiness questionnaire that marks chest symptoms and a recent visit with a physician. What is that health screen supposed to accomplish before training starts?

options.text: Identify risk factors that need clearance or a modification before exercise begins
Diagnose the condition so the trainer can recommend a medication or a change in dose
Produce fitness numbers such as oxygen uptake or a one-rep max before any program is written
Stand in for physician clearance when known heart disease is already written on the form

explanation: The readiness form flags chest symptoms and the recent physician visit so you know this member needs clearance or a change in the plan before training. It is a screen for referral and modification, not a diagnosis and not clearance you can sign.

distractorExplanations.b: Uses the questionnaire to diagnose and to change medication, which a trainer does not do from a form.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a health-history screen with a fitness test such as oxygen uptake or a one-rep max.
distractorExplanations.d: Lets the form replace physician clearance for known heart disease, which is the opposite of what a yes-pattern requires.

prompt: A client cleared after an older episode of low-back pain still rounds sharply on every pull and wants a lifting plan while symptoms stay quiet. What should the programming emphasize now?

options.text: Daily high-rep sit-ups and crunches meant to strengthen the abdominal wall through repetition
Neutral-spine bracing, hip-hinge skill, and gradual exposure to load
Strict rest from every loaded pattern until all discomfort has fully disappeared
Passive stretching into end-range flexion before any bracing or hinging is taught

explanation: With a cleared, quiet history, the pull should be rebuilt around a braced neutral spine and a competent hip hinge, then loaded gradually. The sharp rounding is the pattern to coach, not a reason for crunch volume or forced end-range flexion.

distractorExplanations.a: Piles on spinal-flexion crunches, the repeated bend this history should not use as the main strengthening method.
distractorExplanations.c: Puts a non-acute, cleared client on total rest from load instead of graded exposure to a better hinge.
distractorExplanations.d: Starts with end-range flexion stretching, which provokes the spine before brace and hinge skill are in place.

prompt: After a cardiac event a client finished the supervised hospital phase and brings the cardiologist's written activity limits to the gym. How is this next exercise phase supposed to run?

options.text: Trainer-led zones taken from an age-predicted maximum, with the medical note set aside
Unsupervised home work, on the belief that monitoring ends the moment the hospital discharges the client
Physician-directed work with monitoring, while the trainer stays in scope and follows clearance
Early hard intervals aimed at forcing cardiac output up in the first week back in the gym

explanation: Post-event exercise stays physician-directed and monitored. The cardiologist's written limits are the boundary, and the trainer's job is to work inside that clearance rather than inventing zones or intensity.

distractorExplanations.a: Sets zones from an age formula and sets the cardiologist's note aside, taking over a decision that belongs to the medical team.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats hospital discharge as the end of supervision, so the next phase becomes unmonitored home exercise.
distractorExplanations.d: Starts hard intervals in the first gym week to force cardiac output, ahead of the physician-directed progression.

prompt: At a community center a vigorous grandparent who only strolls the park asks to keep that habit exclusively and skip every strength block for good. What training decision fits an apparently healthy older adult here?

options.text: Keep park strolls as the permanent mode and drop every strength block from the week
Add resistance training progressed so recovery stays intact
Program daily max-effort lifting with no easier week, because age cancels any need to respect recovery between sessions
Cancel the stroll as well until you personally order imaging

explanation: This apparently healthy grandparent should resistance-train, not retire to walking forever. Add strength work and progress it only as far as recovery allows, so the new block is one the client can come back from.

distractorExplanations.a: Locks in walking as the only lifetime mode and skips strength work, which is the miss for a healthy older adult.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds lifting but at daily max effort with no recovery, ignoring the progression the client has to be able to absorb.
distractorExplanations.d: Stops even the stroll and has the trainer order imaging, a clinical step that is not yours to take.

prompt: Late in an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy a member wants the floor crunch from a glossy magazine photo, while the obstetric note already says to modify positions. What should lead the session choice?

options.text: The magazine photo, so the supine crunch stays even though the obstetric note said to change positions
Harder supine drills each week, because an uncomplicated pregnancy removes every positional concern
The physician's guidance, which rules out that late supine crunch
Stopping all prenatal activity for the rest of pregnancy because one magazine crunch looked risky on the page

explanation: The obstetric note leads this session, not the magazine. Late in an uncomplicated pregnancy you do not put the client supine for that crunch just because a photo showed it. Modify the position as the physician directed.

distractorExplanations.a: Lets the magazine photo override the obstetric note and keeps the late supine crunch the note already told you to change.
distractorExplanations.b: Escalates supine work on the idea that an uncomplicated pregnancy erases positional limits the physician already set.
distractorExplanations.d: Cancels all prenatal activity because a photo looked risky, instead of following the guidance that activity may continue with modifications.

prompt: A middle-school group arrives for Saturday practice, and one teen wants the whole hour spent on a single all-out lift so friends can film a record. How should this youth session be built?

options.text: Spend the hour on one filmed max attempt before the pattern has been taught to anyone in the group
Copy an adult percentage chart and load the bar to those numbers on this first Saturday
Remove play and keep adding plates until positions fall apart so the hour feels serious enough
Build skill and play, with loads each teen can control

explanation: This Saturday class should practice skill, include play, and use loads the teens can control. A filmed max-out before the pattern is learned is the session to refuse, even if friends want a record.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns the hour into a max-out film session before anyone has learned the lift, which is the miss for youth practice.
distractorExplanations.b: Loads an adult percentage chart on the first Saturday instead of skill, play, and loads the group can actually control.
distractorExplanations.c: Strips out play and adds plates until form collapses, chasing a serious look rather than controllable practice.

prompt: A prospect marks several yes answers on the readiness form and then asks you to sign the bottom as proof the facility has medically cleared the workout. What does that questionnaire actually accomplish?

options.text: It flags who needs a physician before training; you do not sign clearance
It becomes medical clearance the moment you sign, so the physician visit can be skipped entirely
It diagnoses each yes answer and authorizes you to change the prospect's medicines before the first workout
It replaces the physician and every later symptom check for as long as the membership lasts

explanation: Yes answers on the readiness form tell you this prospect needs a physician before you train them. Your signature does not turn the form into medical clearance, and you do not diagnose or change medicines from those boxes.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats your signature as medical clearance and skips the physician the yes answers were meant to trigger.
distractorExplanations.c: Reads the form as a diagnosis plus permission to change medicines, which a trainer cannot do.
distractorExplanations.d: Lets one questionnaire replace the physician and all future symptom checks for the whole membership.

prompt: Midway through an easy warm-up a client clutches the chest, says the discomfort is new, and asks to finish the set just to see whether the feeling fades. What is the right next action?

options.text: Finish the set first, then decide, because warm-up chest pain often passes if the client keeps pushing
Stop now; do not finish the set to see if it fades
Add a heavier set right away to test whether the new chest pain comes from effort rather than something else
Label it muscle soreness yourself and assign a stretch series instead of ending the session

explanation: New chest pain in the warm-up ends the set immediately. You do not finish the reps to see how it feels, add load to test it, or decide it is soreness. Stop and get the client medical care. You do not diagnose the cause.

distractorExplanations.a: Finishes the set to see if warm-up chest pain passes, which is the delay this symptom does not allow.
distractorExplanations.c: Adds a heavier set as a test, turning new chest pain into an experiment instead of a stop.
distractorExplanations.d: Diagnoses muscle soreness and prescribes stretches, a clinical judgment the trainer does not make.

prompt: A member with known high blood pressure who is already cleared asks you for the exact reading where lifting must cease, then strains hard while holding breath on the first work set. What coaching stays inside your scope?

options.text: Hold the breath and strain hard, because clearance means those spikes no longer matter at all
Teach long breath-holds as the main brace and add a sudden max-strain finisher on the same set
Avoid breath-holding and sudden heavy strain, and invent no pressure cutoff
Publish a personal pressure cutoff you chose today and halt the set only when a cuff matches that private number

explanation: For this cleared member, coach away from breath-holding and sudden heavy strain on the work set. You do not invent a blood-pressure number that decides when lifting stops. That cutoff is not yours to write.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeps the breath-hold and hard strain because clearance is misread as permission for pressure spikes.
distractorExplanations.b: Teaches long breath-holds and a max-strain finisher, which is the sudden strain this client should avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a personal pressure cutoff and uses a cuff reading you chose, a number the trainer must not create.

prompt: A new member living with obesity wants the opening appointment to be an all-out sprint test for a baseline, even though earlier tries ended with joint pain and skipped weeks. What program shape is more useful?

options.text: Open with a maximal sprint test and build a plan if the time looks impressive enough to justify training
Repeat sprints to exhaustion and hold strength work back until a target body weight is reached
Hand over a crash diet you wrote and withhold every session until the next monthly weigh-in
Use resistance work plus activity this client will repeat

explanation: The useful shape is resistance training plus conditioning this member will actually repeat. An all-out sprint test on day one is how earlier weeks got skipped. Do not open there, and do not replace training with a diet you write.

distractorExplanations.a: Opens with a maximal sprint test and ties the whole plan to an impressive time, the start that already caused skipped weeks.
distractorExplanations.b: Repeats sprints to exhaustion and delays strength work for a scale target, skipping the repeatable mix this client needs.
distractorExplanations.c: Substitutes a trainer-written crash diet and withholds sessions, which is outside scope and not a training plan.

prompt: Two weeks after an ankle sprain the clinic note still limits cutting and single-leg loading, yet the client wants to play through the wobble because a match is scheduled Saturday. Which limit should you follow?

options.text: The clinician's limits; do not load a joint that is still unstable
Saturday's match, taping the ankle and adding cutting drills until the wobble feels ordinary again
A max hop test today, overruling the clinic note if a single landing looks acceptable on the floor
A rehab plan you write yourself, replacing the clinician because the sprain looks minor in the gym

explanation: The clinic note still limits cutting and single-leg load, and the ankle is still unstable. Follow those limits. Playing through the wobble for Saturday, or testing it with a max hop, overrides the clinician. You do not replace that care.

distractorExplanations.b: Works through an unstable ankle with cutting drills so a match can happen, ignoring the limits still on the note.
distractorExplanations.c: Uses a max hop to overrule the clinic note when one landing looks fine, substituting your test for the clinician.
distractorExplanations.d: Replaces the clinician with a trainer-written rehab plan because the sprain looks minor, which is outside scope.

prompt: During a crowded circuit a client who has diabetes turns sweaty and shaky, then asks how many insulin units to take before the next station. What is your job in that moment?

options.text: Calculate an insulin dose from the sweating and shakiness and tell the client to inject that amount now
Watch for low blood sugar and give no insulin advice
Ignore the sweaty shaking and finish every remaining station so the circuit log stays complete
Promise that this circuit replaces the physician's diabetes plan and skip any further clinical care

explanation: Sweating and shakiness in this circuit are a signal to watch for low blood sugar and to follow the client's existing care plan. You do not calculate insulin units or tell the client what to inject. Medication advice is not your job.

distractorExplanations.a: Turns sweaty shakiness into an insulin dose you calculate and direct, which is medication advice a trainer must not give.
distractorExplanations.c: Ignores signs of low blood sugar so the circuit log can be finished, leaving the symptom unchecked.
distractorExplanations.d: Replaces the physician's diabetes plan with one circuit, which neither treats the moment nor stays in scope.

prompt: A cleared client with low bone density asks which patterns to keep after a blog banned squats, carries, and every hinge on top of a flexion drill the physician already restricted. What selection fits this case?

options.text: Ban all loading, treating every external resistance as automatically forbidden once bone density is low
Adopt the blog's extra bans and drop squats, carries, and hinges that nobody on the care team restricted
Keep loaded, aligned movement and skip the flexion you were told to avoid
Program high-rep loaded spinal flexion and trade the physician's restriction for the crunch series from the blog

explanation: Choose loaded, well-aligned patterns such as the squats and carries the physician did not ban. Skip the loaded spinal flexion you were told to avoid. Do not grow that restriction into a blog list, and do not put the banned flexion back in.

distractorExplanations.a: Bans every external load, a blanket rule nobody gave, instead of keeping aligned loading the client was cleared to do.
distractorExplanations.b: Copies the blog's extra bans and drops squats, carries, and hinges that were not part of the physician's restriction.
distractorExplanations.d: Swaps the restricted flexion back in as high-rep crunches, overriding the limit you were told to keep.

prompt: A deconditioned beginner stares at a six-day split copied from a magazine, admits the previous calendar died in week two, and asks how many days to schedule. What frequency should open the plan?

options.text: Start at six days because the magazine template outranks a plan that already died in week two
Train seven days at maximal effort so a short streak erases years spent away from the gym
Schedule nothing until a perfect month of meal logs exists, then jump straight to six training days
Start with a frequency they will keep, often two or three days

explanation: This deconditioned beginner already quit a plan in week two, so the opening frequency is one they will keep, often two or three days. A six-day magazine split is not the right start just because the template says six.

distractorExplanations.a: Opens at six days because a magazine said so, repeating the frequency that a plan like this already failed to keep.
distractorExplanations.b: Jumps to seven maximal days to erase years off, which is more than a deconditioned beginner will recover from.
distractorExplanations.c: Withholds training for a month of meal logs, outside your diet scope, then leaps to the same six-day load.

prompt: On a hot gym floor one exerciser stops sweating, seems confused, and says the room is fading, while a partner pushes for another round before anybody drinks. What response belongs in this session?

options.text: Stop now and keep water breaks in the session
Send the client back for another hard round and call the confusion ordinary tiredness from a long day
Remove scheduled water breaks so the class clock never pauses, even when this client is fading
Diagnose the heat illness yourself and decide a medication dose for the client on the gym floor

explanation: Stopped sweating, confusion, or a faint, fading feeling means you stop this client now. Water breaks stay part of the hot-floor session. You do not push another round, pull the water, or diagnose and dose a medicine.

distractorExplanations.b: Sends a confused, fading client who stopped sweating back for another round and renames the signs as ordinary tiredness.
distractorExplanations.c: Removes water breaks to protect the clock, cutting the fluids that belong in a hot session.
distractorExplanations.d: Diagnoses heat illness and picks a medication dose, two clinical decisions a trainer does not make on the floor.

prompt: A physician wrote no overhead pressing after a shoulder flare, and the member asks to keep a light version because the implement will not be heavy. How should you apply that written restriction?

options.text: Allow the light press, because a smaller load cancels a written ban on overhead work
Honor the ban; a light overhead press is still overhead pressing
Turn the ban into a max-effort press once a single warm-up rep feels slightly better than last week
Diagnose the shoulder yourself and delete the restriction from the program card before the session

explanation: No overhead pressing means you modify the session around that ban. A light press is still overhead pressing, so it does not become allowed because the implement is lighter. You do not reinterpret or delete the physician's restriction.

distractorExplanations.a: Rewrites 'no overhead pressing' as 'light overhead pressing is fine,' which overrides the restriction instead of modifying around it.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns the ban into a max-effort press after one easier warm-up rep, escalating past the written limit.
distractorExplanations.d: Diagnoses the shoulder and deletes the physician's restriction, taking over a decision that is not yours.

prompt: Inside a coached group one participant loses the count, the pattern breaks, and everyone else is still on the fast rhythm. What should that participant get from you?

options.text: A shout to catch the count, even though the pattern has already broken down for that person
The same fast load the fittest person is using, so the room never has to split into different levels
The regression, not a shout to catch the tempo
Removal from class for the month, because missing the tempo means this participant cannot train at all

explanation: A group class is still a set of individuals. The participant who lost the tempo and broke the pattern gets a regression they can perform. Shouting to catch the fast count asks them to chase a rhythm their form already missed.

distractorExplanations.a: Shouts at the participant to catch a count the pattern has already lost, instead of changing the exercise to fit them.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeps the fittest person's fast load for everyone so the room looks uniform, ignoring the person who cannot hold the tempo.
distractorExplanations.d: Removes the participant for a month because the tempo was missed, which punishes a coaching problem instead of regressing it.

prompt: Across three straight visits a member reports dizziness plus pain from a fresh tweak and asks for a harder week so the problem gets trained away. Where does your professional scope end?

options.text: At a harder training week, because persistent dizziness and the new pain are problems more load will fix
At a diagnosis you write, followed by treatment sets that take the place of a visit to a licensed clinician
At overriding any physician already involved, if you believe extra load will toughen the symptom over time
At referral to a licensed clinician, not at a harder week

explanation: Persistent dizziness, pain, and a new tweak are the point where your scope ends in a referral to a licensed clinician. A harder week does not train those signs away, and you do not diagnose them or override a physician.

distractorExplanations.a: Answers dizziness and a new injury with a harder week, treating symptoms that need a clinician as a programming gap.
distractorExplanations.b: Ends scope at your own diagnosis and treatment sets, replacing the licensed clinician the client should see.
distractorExplanations.c: Overrides a physician with more load because you think the symptom needs toughening, which is outside your role.

prompt: During a first consult, a well adult wants everyday grocery pointers for herself and, in the same hour, a disease-specific menu for her father who remains under a nephrologist's care. What nutrition work stays inside an ISSA personal trainer's scope?

options.text: General healthy-eating guidelines, with clinical diets referred to a registered dietitian.
A trainer-written kidney menu that replaces the diet orders already set by the nephrology team.
Naming a nutrient deficiency from one visual glance at her father's skin.
Telling her father to pause prescribed medicine so the scale drops faster.

explanation: The consult can cover ordinary healthy-eating guidelines for the adult herself. A disease-specific menu for her father is a clinical diet, so that request goes to a registered dietitian rather than being written in the gym.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses general coaching with medical nutrition therapy. A trainer does not replace the nephrology team's diet orders with a kidney menu.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a visual impression with diagnosis. Naming a deficiency by looking at someone is a clinical judgment, outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses weight talk with medication management. Pausing a prescribed medicine is a physician decision, not a trainer's call.

prompt: At the table, someone logging olive oil, white rice, and grilled chicken asks which of those foods' dominant nutrients packs the most energy into a single gram. Which comparison should you give them?

options.text: Carbohydrate in the rice, at 4 kcal per gram, ahead of the oil.
Fat in the oil, at 9 kcal per gram, ahead of the rice and the chicken.
Protein in the chicken, at 4 kcal per gram, as the densest of the three.
Protein in the chicken counted at 9 kcal per gram, swapped with fat.

explanation: Fat supplies 9 kcal per gram, while carbohydrate and protein each supply 4. On this plate the olive oil, not the rice or the chicken, is the densest energy source in a single gram.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses carbohydrate with fat. Carbohydrate is 4 kcal per gram, so the rice is not denser than the oil.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses protein with fat. Protein is 4 kcal per gram, so the chicken is not the densest of the three.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses protein's energy density with fat's. The 9 kcal per gram figure belongs to fat, not to the chicken's protein.

prompt: Once the lower-body session ends, the lifter wonders why protein still matters if the sets themselves were the signal that told muscle to adapt. What does an adequate protein intake actually contribute in that situation?

options.text: The main fuel for the easier aerobic stretches of that same session.
A glycogen refill that beats carbohydrate after the lifting work.
Amino acids used to repair and remodel the worked muscle tissue.
New muscle even if resistance training is skipped the following week.

explanation: The sets were the signal. Adequate protein contributes amino acids so that worked muscle can be repaired and remodeled. It is not the main fuel for the session, and it does not rebuild glycogen better than carbohydrate.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses protein with the fuels for easier aerobic work. Carbohydrate and fat cover that energy; protein is not the main supply.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses repair with glycogen restoration. Carbohydrate refills glycogen; protein's role here is tissue repair and remodeling.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses building blocks with the training signal. Amino acids do not create new muscle when the resistance work is skipped.

prompt: She keeps postponing food changes with the phrase eat better someday, then asks you to invent a dramatic scale target. What kind of goal makes a habit change more likely to stick?

options.text: An aggressive outcome number you pick so the scale results arrive much faster.
A loose intention left vague so there is no clear mark she could miss.
A final scale figure with no daily action attached to it.
Specific, measurable actions tied to cues and habits in her kitchen.

explanation: Eat better someday cannot be tracked. A habit change is more likely when the goal is specific and measurable and is tied to cues and habits already sitting in her kitchen, rather than a dramatic number you invent.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a trainer-imposed stretch target with adherence. Ownership sits with a specific, measurable action, not a faster outcome you choose.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses flexibility with a usable goal. A vague intention cannot be measured, so it never becomes a habit she can repeat.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the scale outcome with the behavior. Without a daily action and a kitchen cue, the final number has nothing to drive it.

prompt: The front-desk supervisor wants this member's health history and progress photos copied into a staff meeting packet. What does confidentiality require you to do with that personal file?

options.text: Protect health and training information from unauthorized disclosure.
Release the forms if a manager or her employer asks to see them.
Lock the medical history in a drawer, and pass the progress photos around the desk freely.
Shred the whole file after the session so nothing remains stored.

explanation: Health history and progress photos are personal training information. Confidentiality means you protect that file from disclosure to people who were not authorized, including a staff meeting that the member did not approve.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a workplace request with permission. A manager or employer does not get health or training records without the member's authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses medical history with the rest of the file. Progress photos are personal information too and are not free to circulate.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses privacy with destruction. Confidentiality means securing the record, not shredding the file the moment the session ends.

prompt: Opening a small studio means deciding how you will sell blocks of sessions, describe outcomes, and write agreements. Which set of habits belongs in a professional personal-training business?

options.text: Handshake deals, promised transformations, and scope that shifts as needed.
Clear written contracts, truthful marketing, and documented scope limits.
Condition-specific meal plans added so the service list looks larger.
Dropping current CPR and AED cards because liability insurance is active.

explanation: A professional studio runs on clear contracts, marketing that tells the truth about outcomes, and scope limits written down. Those habits define the business before the first block of sessions is sold.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses flexibility with professional practice. Promised transformations and undocumented handshake deals raise liability instead of defining the business.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a longer menu with staying in scope. Meal plans for medical conditions are dietetics practice, not a CPT add-on.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses insurance with emergency readiness. An active policy does not replace a current CPR and AED credential.

prompt: He argues both for and against morning walks, and you feel the pull to talk him into your plan. Which stance matches the spirit of motivational interviewing in that conversation?

options.text: Direction, persuasion, tight accountability, and a corrective lecture.
Expert instruction, correction, and holding him to the trainer's plan.
Partnership, acceptance, compassion, and evocation of his own reasons.
Empathy paired with unsolicited advice, reassurance, and persuasion.

explanation: He is already voicing both sides. Motivational interviewing stays in partnership, acceptance, compassion, and evocation so his own reasons for the walks come forward, instead of you talking him into the plan.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the righting reflex with MI spirit. Directing, persuading, and lecturing are what evocation is meant to replace in this conversation.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an expert-led plan with MI. Instruction and correction put the trainer's agenda ahead of reasons he has not yet said aloud.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses empathy with the whole spirit. Unsolicited advice and persuasion work against evocation even when the tone stays kind.

prompt: Midafternoon heat finds a runner lightheaded after skipping fluids since breakfast, and she asks how that deficit will change the workout. How does dehydration tend to impair performance in this setting?

options.text: Lowering heart rate at a given pace because blood volume dropped.
Raising plasma volume and pushing the sweat rate higher in the heat.
Cutting strength mainly, with little change in endurance or heat tolerance.
Raising cardiovascular strain and reducing tolerance for the heat.

explanation: Skipping fluids since breakfast leaves her low on blood volume in the heat. Dehydration tends to raise cardiovascular strain and reduce heat tolerance, which is why the lightheaded runner should not be coached as if the deficit were harmless.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the heart-rate direction. A smaller blood volume raises heart rate at a given pace; it does not lower it.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses dehydration with extra fluid. Plasma volume falls, and sweat rate eventually drops, which is why heat tolerance worsens.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the systems that suffer most. Endurance and heat tolerance take the hit; this is not a strength-only problem.

prompt: A tub on the counter claims it cures joint disease, and she wants you to endorse that promise before training starts. How should a trainer handle a supplement marketed with a disease-cure claim?

options.text: Avoid the disease-treatment claim, stay evidence-cautious, and refer her to a clinician.
Repeat the cure language if that tub is sold in an ordinary grocery aisle before the session.
Assure her that powders using cure language have been approved as drugs.
Diagnose the joint problem yourself so the tub is easier to endorse.

explanation: A disease-cure line on a tub is not a training cue. Stay evidence-cautious, do not repeat the treatment claim, and send her to a qualified clinician instead of endorsing the promise before the session.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses retail availability with evidence. A grocery shelf does not make a disease-cure claim safe for a trainer to repeat.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a supplement with an approved drug. Cure language on a powder is not FDA drug approval, and you should not imply that it is.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses coaching with diagnosis. Naming her joint problem so you can endorse the tub is outside scope and ethically backwards.

prompt: You need to learn why step targets landed on some days and slipped on others, without forcing a yes or no. Which of these questions is actually open-ended?

options.text: Did you reach the step target on most days this week?
What made hitting your steps easier on the days you succeeded?
Is an evening walk easier for you than a morning walk?
Will you promise a fixed step total every day starting tomorrow?

explanation: An open question invites an explanation. Asking what made the step target easier on the days it worked lets the client describe the conditions, instead of trapping the week in a yes or no.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a yes-or-no check with an open question. Did you reach the target can be answered without explaining what helped.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an either-or choice with an open question. Evening versus morning still boxes the client into two options you named.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a commitment push with curiosity. A promise starting tomorrow is closed, and it sets your number rather than exploring theirs.

prompt: A night-shift employee has managed about five hours of sleep each night for a month and hopes lifting quality will stay intact. What does chronic sleep restriction tend to do?

options.text: Improve fat loss by lowering cortisol and the hormones that drive appetite.
Shift mood and focus while recovery and strength stay the same.
Impair tissue recovery, hormone regulation, and training performance.
Disappear once extra coffee is added, with no loss of session quality.

explanation: A month of short sleep is a recovery problem, not a harmless schedule quirk. Chronic restriction tends to impair recovery, hormone regulation, and training performance, so lifting quality should not be expected to stay intact.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses short sleep with a fat-loss aid. Restricted sleep tends to raise appetite drive, not lower cortisol in a way that improves fat loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses mood with the whole cost. Recovery and performance change too; strength and tissue repair do not sit this out.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a stimulant with restored sleep. Coffee can mask sleepiness and still leave recovery and training quality unrepaired.

prompt: Someone newly diagnosed with celiac disease asks you to build every weekly menu so gluten stays out of breakfast, lunch, and dinner. What should the personal trainer do with that request?

options.text: Write every gluten-free menu yourself, since general healthy eating is treated as in scope.
Suggest a store enzyme so small servings of gluten become acceptable.
Assign a low-carbohydrate week, since dropping most grains manages celiac.
Refer celiac medical nutrition therapy to an RD or physician and stay outside dietetics.

explanation: A weekly menu for diagnosed celiac disease is medical nutrition therapy, not a general grocery chat. Refer that plan to a registered dietitian or physician and do not practice dietetics by writing it yourself.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses general healthy eating with a disease menu. Scope covers ordinary guidance, not a gluten-free prescription for diagnosed celiac disease.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an enzyme product with safe treatment. Enzymes do not make gluten acceptable in celiac disease, and recommending them is outside CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a low-carbohydrate pattern with celiac care. Managing celiac is strict gluten avoidance directed by a dietitian, not a grain cut you assign.

prompt: Before the first workout, your insurer wants to know which habits make harm and a lawsuit less likely. Which practice actually lowers a trainer's liability risk?

options.text: Screen, document, obtain informed consent, and refer red-flag findings.
Rely on the insurance policy and skip the written screening notes.
Accept a spoken waiver in the lobby in place of a signed informed-consent form.
Interpret worrying symptoms in-house so a referral can be skipped.

explanation: Liability drops when the first workout is preceded by screening, written documentation, informed consent, and referral of red flags. The insurer is asking about those habits, not about a shortcut that skips the record.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses coverage with risk reduction. A policy may respond to a claim; it does not replace screening notes that keep the claim from arising.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a conversation with proof. A spoken waiver is hard to show later; signed informed consent is the documented step.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses keeping the client in-house with lowering risk. Interpreting symptoms yourself widens liability and skips the referral red flags need.

prompt: Formal workouts and the food log have not changed, yet weight starts moving after she parks farther away and takes the stairs at work. Which part of daily energy use are those extra steps?

options.text: Resting metabolism, the energy used at complete rest for basic functions.
NEAT, calories burned by daily movement outside formal exercise.
The thermic effect of food, energy used to digest and absorb a meal.
EPOC, calories burned after a workout while the body recovers.

explanation: The workouts and the food log did not change. Parking farther away and taking stairs are daily movement outside formal exercise, which is NEAT, and that extra expenditure is what started the weight moving.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses NEAT with resting metabolism. Energy used at complete rest for basic functions is a different slice of daily expenditure.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses movement with digestion. The thermic effect of food is the cost of processing a meal, not the stairs or the longer walk from the car.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses everyday steps with the after-effect of a workout. EPOC follows formal exercise; these steps were never a planned session.

prompt: Drafting an advertisement for your packages, you must decide which photos and promises are fair to publish. What should ethical advertising for training services avoid?

options.text: Any client story at all, including testimonials that were shared with written consent.
Listing package prices, which certified trainers are barred from showing.
Manipulated before-and-after photos and miracle claims that cannot be verified.
Naming the certification, because that wording implies a medical license.

explanation: The ad can be specific and still honest. Ethical advertising avoids manipulated before-and-after photos and miracle claims that nobody can verify, because those promises are not a fair description of training services.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a consented story with a fake one. A testimonial the client agreed to share is allowed; manipulation and unverifiable miracles are the problem.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses secrecy with ethics. Publishing the price you actually charge is straightforward; certification does not bar trainers from listing it.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a credential line with a medical claim. Naming a CPT certification accurately is expected and does not imply a medical license.

prompt: Three separate asks show up together: ordinary plate ideas for a well adult, a renal menu, and guidance for a client being treated for an eating disorder. Which of those asks can you keep?

options.text: Keep every ask, including the renal menu and the eating-disorder plan, because food talk belongs in every CPT visit.
Keep the eating-disorder plan if you have read about it, and the renal menu if recent labs look calm enough to you.
General healthy eating for the well adult stays in scope; renal and eating-disorder diets go to a registered dietitian.
Keep the renal menu and the eating-disorder plan, and turn away ordinary plate ideas as if those were the clinical work.

explanation: Ordinary plate ideas for a well adult are general healthy eating and can stay with you. A renal diet and an eating-disorder plan are clinical nutrition, so both go to a registered dietitian rather than into the training week.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses any food conversation with full scope. Writing a renal menu or an eating-disorder plan is medical nutrition, not a standard CPT visit.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses self-study or a glance at labs with a license. Reading about an eating disorder or judging labs does not move those diets into CPT scope.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses which ask is in scope. General healthy eating stays; the renal diet and the eating-disorder plan are the ones that leave.

prompt: Butter and chicken sit on the same label, and he insists the chicken must win because protein is the densest energy source per gram. Which densities correct that arithmetic?

options.text: Protein is 9 kcal per gram and fat is 4, so the chicken grams outrank the butter on that label.
Fat is 9 kcal per gram; carbohydrate and protein are 4, so the butter outranks the chicken per gram.
Carbohydrate is 9 kcal per gram, which is why a starch beats butter when you compare one gram.
Fat, carbohydrate, and protein each yield 7 kcal per gram, so the label grams can be compared as equals.

explanation: Protein is not the densest energy source. Fat is 9 kcal per gram, and carbohydrate and protein are 4, so the butter's fat outranks the chicken's protein gram for gram on that label.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses protein with fat and swaps the numbers. Protein is 4 kcal per gram, not 9, so the chicken does not outrank the butter that way.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses carbohydrate with fat. Carbohydrate is 4 kcal per gram, not 9, so a starch does not beat butter on a per-gram basis.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses all three yields with alcohol's 7 kcal per gram. Fat, carbohydrate, and protein are not equal, and none of them is 7.

prompt: Minutes before a morning lift he holds up a pre-workout tub and asks to skip breakfast for a scoop, plus the amount that works. What is the sound coaching response?

options.text: Skip breakfast for the scoop on lifting mornings and pick the larger serving printed toward the top of the label.
Drop the meal whenever the tub is used, because the powder already covers the same jobs as breakfast.
Make the tub the whole morning meal and raise the serving if the first sets feel flat that day.
Keep the real meal pattern, breakfast included; a supplement is not a substitute, and you do not set a dose.

explanation: The tub does not stand in for breakfast. A supplement is not a substitute for a meal pattern, and naming the amount that works would be prescribing a dose, which this coaching response does not do.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a scoop with breakfast and then picks an amount. Replacing the meal and choosing a serving is the opposite of keeping the pattern and refusing a dose.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a powder with a meal. The tub does not cover what breakfast is doing, so skipping food for it is not a sound swap.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a flat warm-up with a reason to raise the serving. Using the tub as the meal and changing the amount is still dose-setting outside the meal pattern.

prompt: She ignored thirst until evening, then emptied a one-gallon jug because a podcast said anything less means a failed day. What hydration message fits a personal trainer's scope here?

options.text: Spread fluid through the day instead of one late chug; a gallon-or-fail rule is not the standard.
Empty a full gallon every day or the day does not count, no matter the climate, body size, or thirst.
Wait until the session starts, then match whatever the largest person in the room happens to drink.
Ignore fluids until after the workout, then treat evening thirst as the only cue that matters.

explanation: Chugging a gallon at night because a podcast called the day a failure is not the lesson. Hydration is fluid spread across the day, and a single gallon-or-fail rule is not the standard you teach.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a podcast slogan with a rule. Requiring a gallon regardless of climate, size, or thirst is the miss, not the hydration message.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses someone else's bottle with a plan. Copying the largest person's intake at the session ignores fluid needs across the rest of the day.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses one thirst cue with the whole day. Waiting until after the workout leaves the hours she already skipped unaddressed.

prompt: A vendor offers commission if your clients buy a tea that claims to flush fat during the two weeks before a photo day. How should you treat that product pitch?

options.text: Take the commission and describe the tea as a two-week fat-loss plan leading into the photo day.
Stock the tea as a post-session recovery drink, treating the flush as refueling after training.
Turn down the offered commission; do not sell that detox tea as a fat-loss product for photo week.
Let clients purchase it on their own, then copy the flush-fat claim into your session notes as coaching.

explanation: Commission and a photo deadline do not make a flush claim true. You do not sell a detox tea as fat loss; that pitch sits outside both the evidence and a trainer's scope.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a commission with permission. Describing the tea as a two-week fat-loss plan repeats a claim you should not sell.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a flush story with recovery. Stocking the tea as refueling still treats a detox product as something you program.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses staying off the sale with staying off the claim. Writing the flush-fat line into session notes is still endorsing it.

prompt: On the way out she asks for the nutrition program, and the easy line in your mouth is just eat cleaner, with no next step. What counts as a real behavior-change plan?

options.text: The slogan eat cleaner, left broad so she can interpret it however she likes until the next visit.
One specific next action she can carry out before the next visit; the slogan eat cleaner is not a program.
A promise to overhaul every meal at once, offered as motivation rather than a single action she can do tomorrow.
Watching the scale alone, with no defined food action between this goodbye and the following session.

explanation: Eat cleaner is not a program. A behavior-change plan is a specific next action she can carry out, named before she leaves, rather than a slogan with nothing to do next.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a slogan with a plan. Eat cleaner can mean anything, so it never becomes the next action she was asking for.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a total overhaul with one next step. Motivation to change every meal at once still leaves tomorrow unspecified.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an outcome check with a behavior. A scale reading without a food action is not the program she asked for on the way out.

prompt: In the lobby a prospect signs the liability waiver and says that signature is enough to start squatting today. What still has to happen before the first workout?

options.text: Nothing further, because a signed waiver already replaces the health questions on a PAR-Q.
A payment receipt, since the legal paper and the medical screen are treated as the same document.
A photo release, which is treated as covering both image rights and the pre-participation health screen.
Complete a PAR-Q health screen before the first squat; the signed waiver is not that medical screen.

explanation: The lobby signature allocates risk. It is not a medical screen. A PAR-Q still has to happen before the first squat, because a waiver does not ask the health questions that screen is for.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a waiver with a PAR-Q. Signing away liability does not replace the health questions that still need answers today.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses payment with screening. A receipt shows the session was bought; it is not the medical screen, and it is not the same document as the waiver.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a publicity form with a health screen. Permission to use photos does not cover pre-participation questions.

prompt: Waist numbers and progress pictures are ready to publish, and a prospect asks if joining guarantees that same change. Where is the ethical line on privacy and results?

options.text: Keep her waist measurements private; a consented before-and-after you publish is not a promise of the same result.
Publish the waist numbers and photos without asking, and tell prospects they will match that same change on a set date.
Share the numbers in a public story because transformation posts are ordinary, and treat the pictured change as a promise.
Use the photos in ads once any waiver is signed, and guarantee the next client the same clothing change.

explanation: Waist numbers stay private. A before-and-after can go up only with that client's consent, and even then it is not a promise that the prospect will get the same change by joining.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a marketing urge with consent. Posting measurements and photos without asking, then promising the same result, breaks both privacy and honesty.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a common post with permission. Ordinary transformation stories still need consent, and the pictured change is not a guarantee.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a liability waiver with a photo release and a promise. A waiver does not authorize the ad, and the same clothing change cannot be guaranteed.

prompt: The trial hour was billed at the price you quoted, then a new assessment line appears on the invoice after she has already paid. Where did the pricing practice go wrong?

options.text: It failed because every trial hour must be free, so any charge at all breaks the pricing rules trainers are held to.
It failed because an assessment can be billed only through a physician's office, never on a training invoice.
Charge the price you quoted to her before the trial; the surprise assessment fee after she paid is the miss.
It did not fail; adding a fee after the hour is fine whenever the work ran longer than the quote suggested.

explanation: The quote was the price. Adding an assessment fee after she has already paid is the miss, because pricing is what you said it was before the trial hour, not a new line on the way out.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a surprise add-on with a ban on charging. The trial can have a price; the failure is changing that price after the session.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a trainer's assessment with a medical bill. The problem is not which office prints the invoice; it is the fee she was never told about.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a longer hour with permission to reprice. Running long does not justify a surprise assessment line after she has paid the quoted price.

prompt: Living with diabetes, he wants you to change his medication timing around workouts so you, not the prescriber, are directing treatment. Where does a personal trainer's line sit?

options.text: Change the medication timing yourself once you have watched several of his workouts and feel familiar with the schedule.
Refer him out to his prescriber; directing the diabetes medication is treatment that sits past a CPT's line.
Rewrite the medication timing in the program notes and review that change together at the next session.
Keep the medication role and also write the clinical meal pattern, since both jobs sit inside personal training.

explanation: He is asking you to direct treatment. Managing diabetes medication sits past the CPT line, so you refer that goal out to the prescriber instead of adjusting the timing around his workouts.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses familiarity with authority. Watching his workouts does not give you license to change when diabetes medication is taken.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a program note with a prescription. Writing a new medication time into the plan is still directing treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses two out-of-scope jobs with the CPT role. Medication management and a clinical meal pattern both belong with licensed clinicians.

prompt: Two glasses of wine are being penciled into the evening as a recovery drink that supposedly helps muscles after lifting. How should you classify alcohol in that plan?

options.text: Alcohol is 4 kcal per gram like carbohydrate, and a programmed glass counts as a recovery serving after lifting.
Alcohol is 9 kcal per gram like fat, so you should schedule the wine as the post-lift recovery drink.
Alcohol provides no usable energy, so two glasses can sit in the evening plan as a calorie-free recovery aid.
Alcohol is 7 kcal per gram, and those evening glasses are not a recovery tool you program after lifting.

explanation: Wine does not belong in the plan as a recovery drink. Alcohol is 7 kcal per gram, and it is not a recovery tool you program after lifting, whatever the evening ritual suggests.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses alcohol with carbohydrate. Alcohol is 7 kcal per gram, not 4, and a glass is not a recovery serving you write into the plan.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses alcohol with fat. The 9 kcal figure belongs to fat; alcohol is 7, and scheduling it as the recovery drink is still the miss.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses alcohol with a zero-energy drink. Those glasses carry 7 kcal per gram, and they are not a calorie-free recovery aid.

prompt: Immediately after the last set he worries repair will stall unless the protein comes from one branded shaker sold at the counter. What is the accurate point to coach?

options.text: Protein after training supports muscle repair, and that protein need not be a branded counter shake.
Repair waits on that counter shaker; protein from ordinary food after training does not do the same job.
Skip protein after training, because the session itself finishes repair without any food afterward.
A branded shaker replaces the need for protein at other meals across the rest of the day.

explanation: Repair does not wait on a logo. Protein after training supports repair, and that protein can come from food; it does not have to be the branded shaker sold at the counter.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a brand with the nutrient. Food protein after training supports repair; the counter shaker is not a requirement.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the session with the building material. The sets are the signal, and protein afterward still supports repair.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses one post-training serving with the whole day. A shaker does not erase the need for protein at other meals.

prompt: She will sign the agreement only if a dress size is promised by the wedding date printed on the calendar. What can you honestly put in that contract?

options.text: A written guarantee that she will be one dress size smaller by the wedding if she attends the sessions.
The size and the wedding date, as long as the contract calls that line a goal instead of a guarantee.
Do not guarantee her a clothing size by the wedding date she wants written into the contract.
A refund that pays out unless the promised size is reached on that exact wedding date.

explanation: The wedding date does not make a dress size predictable. You do not guarantee a clothing size by a calendar date, so that promise does not go into the agreement, whatever she needs in order to sign.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses attendance with a result you can promise. Showing up for sessions still does not let you guarantee a dress size by the wedding.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a softer label with honesty. Calling the size-and-date line a goal does not make a clothing promise something you can put in the contract.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a refund clause with permission. Paying out unless the size arrives still treats that size and date as a promise.

prompt: After you sent someone to a clinician and wrote up the hour, a coworker says the group chat is a sufficient record. Where should those notes actually live?

options.text: In the group chat, because a message thread replaces a client file for sessions and referrals.
Keep them in the business file of sessions and referrals; a coworker group chat is not that file.
Nowhere permanent, because writing down a referral creates more liability than keeping the story verbal.
On a public social post so other trainers can see the referral trail and the notes from that hour.

explanation: The referral and the session write-up are business records. They belong in the file you keep for sessions and referrals. A group chat is not that file, even if the coworker can scroll back to the message.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a chat thread with the client record. Messages among coworkers do not replace the file of sessions and referrals.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses documentation with extra risk. The referral note is part of running the business; leaving it unwritten is the gap.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a record with publicity. A public post exposes the referral and the session instead of filing them.

prompt: Renewal paperwork is almost due, and a peer says you may let the credential lapse and still coach people under that title. What keeps the certification in force?

options.text: Letting it lapse and still coaching under that title, since the people who already train with you know your name.
Skipping renewal and posting the old title, because years of experience replace the need to keep the credential current.
Coaching under the lapsed name while you decide later whether finishing the renewal is worth the effort.
Continuing education is what keeps that certification current; a lapsed title is not yours to keep using.

explanation: The title stays yours while the certification stays current. Continuing education is what keeps it in force. Letting the credential lapse and still coaching people under that title is the miss.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses client familiarity with a current credential. People knowing your name does not let you keep using a title after it lapses.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses experience with renewal. Years of coaching do not replace continuing education, and the old title cannot stay on the post.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a delay with staying certified. Coaching under the lapsed name while you think about renewal is still using a title you no longer hold.
